intro: Every AI decision is a trade-off. Make the calls, see the consequences, and discover why humanitarian principles matter in every choice.
principlesHeading: What your choices are measured against
recordSummary: Combined results across {n} completed scenario(s). Replay with different choices to see how the balance shifts.
footerNote: All scenarios and characters are fictional. Content and terminology are inspired by the Red Cross Red Crescent Movement’s ICT Resolution (preparecenter.org/site/ict-resolution) and by scenario-based humanitarian learning games such as “In 90 Days” and “Mission Zhobia” (humanitariangames.com).
takeawayHeading: Questions to take back to your team
takeaways: Who is accountable when an automated system harms an affected person — and can they switch it off?
Could you explain, to the community and to a journalist, exactly who holds people’s data and why?
Whose needs are invisible to your data — and who checks the model’s blind spots?
If your cloud or AI vendor changed its terms, was acquired, or became linked to a party in a conflict, could you exit — and how fast?
Before any AI tool launches, who assesses the harm it could do to affected communities — and are those communities part of the assessment?
What energy, water, and connectivity does the tool demand — and who bears that cost?
Where does a human sign, on the record, before an algorithm’s recommendation becomes someone’s reality?

codeIntro: Everything the game says lives in these files. This page renders the live data exactly as deployed — download it, edit it in any text editor, and your edits ship with the next deploy.

principles.name: Humanity
principles.description: Prevent and alleviate suffering, protect life and health, and ensure respect for every person.

principles.name: Impartiality
principles.description: Help based on need alone, without discrimination as to nationality, gender, belief, or status.

principles.name: Neutrality
principles.description: Take no sides in hostilities or in political, racial, religious, or ideological controversies.

principles.name: Independence
principles.description: Remain autonomous from governments, companies, and other interests so action stays humanitarian.

principles.name: Do No Harm & Accountability
principles.description: ICT Resolution commitments: protect data, engage and answer to communities, procure ethically, and avoid or mitigate harm to affected people.

modeSoloHint: Make the calls yourself, at your own pace.
modeWorkshopHint: One shared screen. The group discusses, votes and decides together.
selectFirst: Tap an option to select it
exitConfirm: Leave this scenario? Your progress so far is saved.
discussPrompts: Who benefits from each option — and who could be harmed?
What data would be used, and is any of it sensitive?
Is AI actually needed here, or would something simpler work?
What would it cost in energy, water and hardware?
Where do humans stay in charge — and how could people challenge the outcome?
timeUp: Time is up — time to vote
voteHint: Count a show of hands with + and −. The option with the most votes is selected — you can change it.
afterDiscuss: Before moving on: did this match what the group expected? What would you do differently?
guideSteps: Plan 60–90 minutes for 4–20 people. Put the game on a big screen or projector.
Pick one or two scenarios that fit your team's work. Read the role and situation aloud.
For each decision: read the situation, discuss for a few minutes with the timer, then vote by show of hands.
Read the consequence and 'why it matters' together, and pause on the discussion question.
Finish with the debrief and the questions for your team. Download the summary to share afterwards.
guideNote: Nothing is sent anywhere: votes and results stay on this device.
